title: You cannot see the seer
hookLine: a practical man demands to be shown the self the way you'd point at a cow, and hears why it can never be pointed to
carry: the self is the seer, never the seen
tomorrow: the next man asks the same question, word for word. same answer?
last: YOUR BREATH IS THE WORLD'S BREATH.

lines: A MAN WHO SURVIVED ON LEFTOVER BEANS.
cards: A man starving in a famine eats leftover beans from an elephant driver to stay alive. Then the driver offers him water, and he turns it down: water, he says, I can find anywhere.
That's Ushasti Chakrayana, in the Chandogya we read last month. Some readers take him to be today's challenger, Ushasta Chakrayana. Whoever he is, he's practical.
He doesn't want theory. He wants to be shown. Point to it, he says, the way you'd point to a cow.

teach.h: SHOW ME THE SELF WITHIN ALL.
teach.b: Yajnavalkya, he says, explain to me the Brahman that is right here, direct, not secondhand: the self that is within everything. That is your self, Yajnavalkya answers, within everything. Which one?
The one that breathes in with your in-breath and out with your out-breath. That is your self, within all.

teach.h: NOT LIKE POINTING AT A COW.
teach.b: Ushasta isn't having it. You've explained it the way someone says, that's a cow, that's a horse. I asked for the direct one.
And here Yajnavalkya gives the answer this day is named for: na drishter drashtaram pashyeh.

teach.h: YOU CANNOT SEE THE SEER OF SEEING.
teach.b: You cannot see the seer of seeing. You cannot hear the hearer of hearing. You cannot think the thinker of thinking.
You cannot know the knower of knowing. That is your self, within all. Everything else is sorrow.
This is the atman, the self, as the Upanishads teach it.
Everything you can point to is something seen. The self isn't something seen. It's what's doing the seeing.
Your eye sees the whole room and never once sees itself. For Yajnavalkya, that doesn't make the self far away. It makes it nearer than anything you could point to.
And it changes an ordinary day. We look at faces, screens, our own reflection, and quietly ask which of them is me. The Upanishad's answer: none of them.

how: Teachers of Advaita Vedanta use this passage in self-inquiry, inviting students to turn attention back toward the one who sees; commentators of several Vedanta schools discuss the line about the seer of seeing.

o: the herdsman who drove the cows home
the elephant driver who shared his beans
the man who asked for the self, pointed out

games.q: what's inside the exchange — tap the pairs.
p: show me the self, like a cow
the one who breathes in and out
you cannot see the seer of seeing

s: Ushasta is satisfied with Yajnavalkya's first answer
he says it's like pointing at a cow or a horse, and asks again.
Yajnavalkya says the seer of seeing can't be seen
you cannot see the seer of seeing, hear the hearer of hearing.
a man of nearly the same name appears in the Chandogya
Ushasti Chakrayana, who survived a famine on leftover beans.

games.q: your little cousin asks: 'if i have a soul, where is it? point to it.' by Yajnavalkya's answer to Ushasta, what fits?
o: you can't point to it, because it's the one doing the looking.
it's in your chest, near your heart, like an organ.
nowhere: if you can't point to it, it isn't real.
games.why: you cannot see the seer of seeing. the self isn't one more thing to point at; it's the one pointing. Ushasta falls silent.

practice: Hindu teachers call this self-inquiry. With your eyes open and soft, notice what you see, then gently try to turn around and find the one who's seeing; you won't find it as a thing.
Close your eyes and do the same with sounds: hear, and then look for the hearer. Don't strain; rest in not finding it, and in the seeing still going on.

wordCard.voice: Ushasta. The man who wanted the self pointed out like a cow, and heard about the drashta, the seer, who can never be seen, because it is the one looking.

orig.note: Sanskrit draṣṭṛ (nominative draṣṭā): the seer, from dṛś, to see.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: the self is the seer, never the seen. Tomorrow, the same question asked again, word for word. Day three hundred seventy-five, done.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.10–11 (Ushasti Chakrayana in the famine)
